brave.title: Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
brave.snippet:
We decomposed two annual embedding products into named features and verified them against external reference data. By doing so, we found that annual Earth embeddings are interpretable records of the land surface. They record abrupt canopy change, resolve its severity, and date it to the calendar year containing the first growing season after the disturbance.
Do Earth embeddings contain features that correspond to identifiable surface phenomena and can be verified against independent maps? If so, what do those features record about a disturbance, such as when it occurred, how severe it was or what caused it? And do different embedding products, trained on largely the same observations of Earth, contain the same phenomena? Here we decompose the two publicly available global embedding products, Tessera [8] and AlphaEarth [9], with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) [27, 28], a method developed to interpret language models.
Supplementary Information Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
The embeddings record what a disturbance did to the surface, not what caused it, so they separate causes only when the surfaces differ. Fire does leave a distinct surface, and accordingly the western US burn family responds to European fires but not to European harvest or windthrow (Supplementary Note S9). Two further experiments demonstrate the temporal limits of decomposing annual embeddings.

# Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
###### Abstract
Earth observation foundation models produce global metre-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet these embeddings are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, which makes them difficult to interpret and their robustness hard to assess. Here, we propose sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a principled way to decompose Earth embeddings into sparse, approximately monosemantic features over an overcomplete dictionary.
Because the standard practice of using LLMs to judge interpretations does not transfer to satellite pixels, and spatial autocorrelation matters, we introduce a tailored evaluation protocol. It scores any SAE on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concepts, and spatial scale, each against baselines that include an SAE whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary. On this protocol, SAEs reconstruct AlphaEarth and Tessera embeddings better than every baseline at matched sparsity.
Their features align with far fewer reference concepts than raw embedding dimensions (on AlphaEarth, 88% align with at most one of 20 concept groups, most with none, against a median of 12 per raw dimension). They also carry more of their variance at fine spatial scales (23 to 32% within a 640 m patch for BatchTopK and Matryoshka, against 9%).
An SAE with a frozen random decoder shares both properties, which therefore follow from sparsity, whereas only a learned dictionary reconstructs the embedding accurately: on AlphaEarth, trained SAEs leave eight times less variance unexplained. We test the sparse code on two applications, discovering land-cover sub-concepts and detecting out-of-distribution pixels by area-of-applicability estimation. Both indicate how sparse features could be used, but neither is yet reliable enough for practical use.

# Earth Embeddings
###### Abstract
Earth observation is moving from foundation models that users must run themselves toward embedding products that package model feature outputs as reusable data without needing to download and process the imagery used to generate them. Earth embeddings are vectors that summarize locations, image patches, or pixels, letting users analyze compact features instead of repeatedly training or running large models on raw satellite imagery. This chapter explains the main types of Earth embeddings, from implicit location encoders to explicit patch and pixel products, and compares their coverage, resolution, dimensionality, storage cost, licenses, and reproducibility.
## 1 Introduction
In Earth observation (EO), this idea is attractive because public EO archives are already at petabyte scale and continue to grow rapidly: for example, NASA’s EOSDIS reported 178.7 PB of archived Earth science data and an average archive growth of 160 TB/day for FY2025 (NASA Earthdata, 2025). In this chapter, we use the term Earth embeddings to refer to reusable vector representations of the Earth system, including implicit location embeddings, patch-level image embeddings, and dense pixel-level embedding products.
## 5 Experiments
Beyond supervised mapping, embeddings may also support similarity search and retrieval, but this use case is less systematically evaluated. Betti et al. (2026) show that implicit location embeddings, including GeoCLIP, SatCLIP, Climplicit, and CSP-fMoW, can be decomposed into human-interpretable representations while retaining high reconstruction capability, revealing interpretable geographic structures such as forests, deserts, roads, landmarks, and urban features. This suggests that implicit embeddings contain monosemantic geographic structure that could support retrieval and geographic search.

# Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
###### Abstract
Earth observation foundation models produce global metre-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet these embeddings are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, which makes them difficult to interpret and their robustness hard to assess. Here, we propose sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a principled way to decompose Earth embeddings into sparse, approximately monosemantic features over an overcomplete dictionary.

## 1 Introduction
Earth embeddings compress petabytes of satellite imagery into compact, reusable vector representations that capture the state of the land surface at any location and time [1].

We bring this approach to Earth embeddings.

Our contributions are as follows:

We apply sparse autoencoders to pixelwise Earth embeddings for the first time, decomposing AlphaEarth and Tessera embeddings into sparse codes over overcomplete dictionaries (Figure 1 a).

We use the term *Earth embedding* for any learned vector representation of a location on Earth [1, 41].

Sparse autoencoders disentangle Earth embeddings into approximately monosemantic geographic features.

# Earth Embeddings

Earth observation is moving from foundation models that users must run themselves toward embedding products that package model feature outputs as reusable data without needing to download and process the imagery used to generate them. Earth embeddings are vectors that summarize locations, image patches, or pixels, letting users analyze compact features instead of repeatedly training or running large models on raw satellite imagery. This chapter explains the main types of Earth embeddings, from implicit location encoders to explicit patch and pixel products, and compares their coverage, resolution, dimensionality, storage cost, licenses, and reproducibility.

In Earth observation (EO), this idea is attractive because public EO archives are already at petabyte scale and continue to grow rapidly: for example, NASA’s EOSDIS reported 178.7 PB of archived Earth science data and an average archive growth of 160 TB/day for FY2025 (NASA Earthdata, 2025). In this chapter, we use the term Earth embeddings to refer to reusable vector representations of the Earth system, including implicit location embeddings, patch-level image embeddings, and dense pixel-level embedding products.

These examples show that geospatial embeddings are not limited to supervised classification: they can also function as compact place descriptors and searchable indexes of the Earth’s surface.

# What's in an Earth Embedding? An Explainability Analysis of Location Encoders
## Abstract
We decompose these embeddings into human-interpretable features\unicode{x2014}namely, (i) sparse latent concepts, (ii) natural language concepts, and (iii) visual features.

## AI Overview
The rapid growth of geospatial data—ranging from satellite imagery to geotagged social media—has prompted the machine learning community to develop general-purpose representations of the Earth's surface. These representations, often called Earth embeddings, are typically generated by "location encoders." These neural networks map geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) to high-dimensional vectors that capture the characteristics of a specific place. While these embeddings are effective for tasks like predicting local climates or identifying species presence, they remain "black boxes."

## Bridging Language and Space via SpLiCE

For model developers, the ability to decompose embeddings into sparse concepts or text terms offers a new pathway for debugging and iterative improvement.

Interpreting clip with sparse linear concept embeddings (splice)

This paper introduces the Sparse Linear Concept Embeddings (SpLiCE) framework, which is one of the three core explainability methods the main paper adapts to decompose location embeddings into predefined natural language concepts.

Because LLM judges of interpretations do not transfer to satellite pixels, and spatial autocorrelation matters, we introduce a tailored evaluation protocol. It scores any SAE on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concepts, and spatial scale, each against baselines that include an SAE whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary. GeoFMs is the term used for large multimodal deep learning systems developed for general- purpose use and trained on diverse geospatial datasets [53] that ingest raw data (e.g., remote sensing imagery, climate records, and socioeconomic layers). Earth embeddings can be produced by many of these models but are more a byproduct of GeoFMs, which are often meant to be fine- tuned for specific downstream tasks, such as satellite image segmentation. A reusable embedding encoder produces vectors for user- supplied inputs, whereas an Earth embedding product publishes precomputed vectors with spatial or temporal indexing. The review focuses on global or near- global Earth embedding products and dis cusses foundation models and reusable encoders where they explain how those products are constructed, evaluated, or used.   

Distributing embeddings rather than only model weights separates large- scale representation inference from taskspecific prediction (Fig. 1). Researchers with labeled observations can fit downstream models without reproducing the original inference workload, while product providers assume the cost of large- area encoding, storage, and updates. Word2Vec [24] and GloVe [25] introduced a comparable separation in natural language processing (NLP) by providing reusable semantic vectors for text analysis. Earth embeddings provide reusable features for geospatial data, while recent products increasingly encode multiple dates and sources rather than a single image. The move toward multitemporal, multisource vectors resembles the transition from static word vectors to contextualized language representations [26].
...
This survey places global and near- global embedding products at the center of the review. It distinguishes precomputed embedding layers and datasets from reusable encoders, compares their input data, spatial and temporal support, dimensionality, and release formats, and examines the infrastructure through which users can obtain or query them. It also relates community benchmarks to published applications and directly compares multiple embeddings through representation geometry, land- cover classification, continuous- variable regression, and sensitivity to embedding dimension. The resulting account connects how Earth embeddings are produced and distributed with how they are evaluated and used, while identifying common requirements for updating, compatibility, and long- term access.

## Abstract

Ecological monitoring, carbon accounting and biodiversity assessment increasingly rely on annual Earth embeddings--learned vectors that compress a year of satellite observation for every ten-meter pixel on Earth, consumed in place of the imagery itself. What these vectors mean has not been established. Here we decompose two widely used embedding products and show that they contain individual ecological features, including fire, forest clearing and crop type, validated against independent reference data on events across six continents. The recovered concepts date abrupt canopy loss to the first post-disturbance growing season and resolve severity well enough to separate prescribed fire from wildfire. Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.

deepseek.snippet:
# Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders

Vitus Benson ⋅ Fanny Yang ⋅ Markus Reichstein
...
Earth observation foundation models produce global meter-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet the embeddings themselves are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, rendering their interpretability and robustness challenging for practitioners and scientists alike. Here, we propose sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a principled way to decompose Earth embeddings into overcomplete dictionaries of sparse, approximately monosemantic features. We introduce an evaluation protocol suited to a domain where LLM-based auto-interpretability fails and spatial autocorrelation matters, scoring any SAE on reconstruction, sparsity, monosemantic recovery, and spatial coherence against a curated label registry of categorical and continuous reference products. On this protocol, three state-of-the-art SAE recipes (ReLU+$\ell_1$, BatchTopK, and Matryoshka BatchTopK) all recover monosemantic and spatially contiguous concepts from AlphaEarth and Tessera embeddings much better than raw embeddings, with Matryoshka the strongest of the three. Two applications follow: (i) unsupervised discovery of land-cover subconcepts (e.g., splitting water into river, lake, ocean), and (ii) improved area-of-applicability estimates for OOD detection. Together, these results are a step toward Earth observation models whose features can be inspected rather than only used, opening pathways for scientific discovery and improved trustworthiness in geospatial applications.

Annual Earth embeddings squeeze a year of satellite observations into one vector for every 10-meter pixel, and people already use them for ecological monitoring and mapping. A downstream model's accuracy, though, doesn't reveal whether a particular phenomenon, such as a fire scar, is actually represented in the vector. The authors' move is to unpack the embedding into sparse, named components and test those components against independent records of what happened on the land. In the central example, a feature family selected on California's 2021 Dixie Fire reproduces its mapped burn scar. That is evidence a surface event can be made visible inside an embedding, though not that every event or every product is equally legible.

![Image 1: Six-panel figure of the Dixie Fire seen through Tessera embeddings](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/paper-figures/01a175de-1142-7c53-ae37-50dbca518544/01a177fb-0aae-7034-8d1b-9b2bc69524ec.png)

The Dixie Fire area as satellite imagery, as a dense 128-dimensional embedding, and after decomposition into separate feature activation maps. The 32-feature burn family's mean activation traces the scar, and its burned-minus-unburned contrast peaks in the first post-fire year, including on three other fires (North Complex, Caldor, Mosquito) where the family was not screened. This is one selected family on one primary example.

An annual Earth embedding is a learned per-pixel vector summarizing a year of satellite data. Its signal for any given event is spread across many dimensions, so no single dimension plainly means "fire." The authors decompose the vectors with a sparse autoencoder, a method that represents each vector using a small number of active directions chosen from a larger learned dictionary. Each direction is a _feature_, and its nonnegative weight at a pixel is its _activation_. For Tessera in the Dixie example, the dictionary has 1,024 features with 16 active per pixel.

_Illustrations by Gus Becker_

Every day, satellites collect enormous amounts of data about the planet: optical imagery, radar, elevation, weather observations, and more.

Traditionally, geospatial analysis has depended on turning that raw data into insights via remote sensing methods, statistical analysis, or computer vision/machine learning techniques. Band indices like NDVI or NDWI, land cover classifications, and statistical summaries help transform imagery into something we can analyze and reason about.

Those approaches still matter. Many are scientifically rigorous, interpretable, and extremely effective for targeted problems.

But a growing class of geospatial models are starting from a different premise. Instead of relying only on human-defined categories or measurements, [foundation models](https://developmentseed.org/blog/2024-11-01-geofm/) learn representations directly from Earth observation data. The outputs of those systems — embeddings — are becoming an increasingly important building block for retrieval, similarity search, clustering, and other emerging geospatial AI workflows.

**If you’ve spent the last year hearing terms like “GeoFM,” “foundation model,” or “embedding” without a clear mental model for how they connect together, this post is for you.**

keenable.snippet: Ecological monitoring, carbon accounting and biodiversity assessment increasingly rely on annual Earth embeddings--learned vectors that compress a year of satellite observation for every ten-meter pixel on Earth, consumed in place of the imagery itself. What these vectors mean has not been established. Here we decompose two widely used embedding products and show that they contain individual ecological features, including fire, forest clearing and crop type, validated against independent reference data on events across six continents. The recovered concepts date abrupt canopy loss to the first post-disturbance growing season and resolve severity well enough to separate prescribed fire from wildfire. Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.

keenable.title: Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
keenable.snippet:
Here we decompose the two publicly available global embedding products, Tessera [8] and AlphaEarth [9], with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) [27, 28], a method developed to interpret language models. An SAE rewrites each embedding as a weighted combination of a few features, chosen from a learned set with many more features than the embedding has dimensions. Because each pixel can use only a few features, each feature tends to specialize on one surface condition, unlike principal components, which mix many. We test whether a feature records a phenomenon by when it appears, since a feature that represents fire should activate on burned pixels in the year of a mapped fire or after, and not before.

We decomposed two annual embedding products into named features and verified them against external reference data. By doing so, we found that annual Earth embeddings are interpretable records of the land surface. They record abrupt canopy change, resolve its severity, and date it to the calendar year containing the first growing season after the disturbance. The findings follow ecological intuition, which is consistent with the decomposition capturing real structure rather than artifacts of the method. Had it produced incoherent features like burn features peaking before fires, or a clean separation of causes that leave identical surface signals, either would have pointed to artifacts of the method. Representations that are already widely used can thus be decomposed into physically interpretable features and checked against independent data.

keenable.title: Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
keenable.snippet:
An annual Earth embedding is a learned per-pixel vector summarizing a year of satellite data. Its signal for any given event is spread across many dimensions, so no single dimension plainly means "fire." The authors decompose the vectors with a sparse autoencoder, a method that represents each vector using a small number of active directions chosen from a larger learned dictionary. Each direction is a *feature*, and its nonnegative weight at a pixel is its *activation*. For Tessera in the Dixie example, the dictionary has 1,024 features with 16 active per pixel.
Training uses embeddings alone, with no labels, reference maps or event dates, so the decomposition is never taught to look for fire.

keenable.title: Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
keenable.snippet:
#### AlphaEarth Foundations
[2] is the model that produced the Google Satellite Embedding dataset, whose D=64 embeddings we use. It treats the imagery of a location as a video: an encoder with spatial and temporal self-attention summarises all observations of a year into one unit-norm embedding per 10 m pixel. During training, decoders reconstruct from this summary the trajectories of many sources over the same period: optical multispectral imagery (Sentinel-2 and Landsat), synthetic-aperture radar (Sentinel-1), GEDI spaceborne lidar, MODIS land-surface temperature, ERA5 climate reanalysis, digital elevation and label maps; the embedding is also aligned with text. To produce the released embeddings, however, the trained encoder is applied to Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery only.

Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.

Title: NeurEO: dissecting Earth observation embeddings with computational neuroscience

Authors: Thijs L van der Plas, Jacob JW Bakermans, Ioannis N Athanasiadis

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Earth embeddings are compressed representations of rich Earth observation data that enable downstream models to tackle a wide range of complex geospatial tasks. Yet, this increase in performance comes at the cost of decreased interpretability, as the semantic meaning of Earth embeddings is unknown. To address this challenge, we borrow methods from the field of computational neuroscience, which aim to interpret activity in (biological) neurons. Here, we adapt and apply these methods to assign meaning to AlphaEarth embeddings. We analyse embedding features both as stand-alone data, equivalent to spontaneous neural activity, and in relation to land cover and elevation correlates, equivalent to stimulus-response neural activity. We demonstrate correlational and multi-scale structure in the embedding features. Embedding features can display highly specific and directional tuning to land cover and elevation, such as a \`North vs South woodland edge' response. When we remove the main trends of combined land cover responses (like water versus land tuning), we discover fine-grained representational details with increased effective dimensionality. Together, our analyses start to unravel what these Earth embeddings represent, which is critical for developing trustworthy downstream applications.

octen.title: A Primer for Earth Data Embeddings — Development Seed
octen.snippet:
Embeddings are one way we make use of the rich representations learned by geospatial foundation models, supporting everything from search and retrieval to natural language interfaces. Yet for many practitioners, the concept remains opaque. This primer explores how embeddings are generated, the kinds of questions they help answer, and why they’re useful across the geospatial ecosystem.
 
Illustrations by Gus Becker
Every day, satellites collect enormous amounts of data about the planet: optical imagery, radar, elevation, weather observations, and more.
Traditionally, geospatial analysis has depended on turning that raw data into insights via remote sensing methods, statistical analysis, or computer vision/machine learning techniques. Band indices like NDVI or NDWI, land cover classifications, and statistical summaries help transform imagery into something we can analyze and reason about.
 
Those approaches still matter. Many are scientifically rigorous, interpretable, and extremely effective for targeted problems.
But a growing class of geospatial models are starting from a different premise. Instead of relying only on human-defined categories or measurements, foundation models learn representations directly from Earth observation data. The outputs of those systems — embeddings — are becoming an increasingly important building block for retrieval, similarity search, clustering, and other emerging geospatial AI workflows.
If you’ve spent the last year hearing terms like “GeoFM,” “foundation model,” or “embedding” without a clear mental model for how they connect together, this post is for you.
The illustrations throughout this post—and the accompanying downloadable poster and mini-zine— use a crocheting metaphor to visualize a core idea behind geospatial foundation models and embeddings: transforming large volumes of raw Earth observation data into reusable representations that can support many downstream tasks and workflows.

Earth observation foundation models produce global metre-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet these embeddings are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, which makes them difficult to interpret and their robustness hard to assess. Here, we propose sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a principled way to decompose Earth embeddings into sparse, approximately monosemantic features over an overcomplete dictionary . Because LLM judges of interpretations do not transfer to satellite pixels, and spatial autocorrelation matters, we introduce a tailored evaluation protocol. It scores any SAE on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concepts, and spatial scale, each against baselines that include an SAE whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary.

perplexity.snippet:
Geographic implicit neural representations (INRs) learn to map any coordinate on Earth to a location embedding, implicitly encoding geospatial data into the weights of a neural network.
Location embeddings are widely used off the shelf as general-purpose geospatial representations, yet users lack principled tools to audit what geographic or semantic information these embeddings capture.
In this work, we analyze the information content of geographic INRs through their location embeddings.
We decompose these embeddings into human-interpretable features—namely, (i) sparse latent concepts, (ii) natural language concepts, and (iii) visual features.
The latent concept embeddings are learned using sparse autoencoders.
To recover natural language concepts, we apply sparse linear concept embeddings (SpLiCE) over a predefined geospatial dictionary.
Finally, visual features are extracted using saliency maps derived from CLIP Surgery.
We show that location embeddings can be decomposed into human-interpretable representations while retaining high reconstruction capability, revealing interpretable geographic structures such as forests, deserts, and urban features.
Across methods, sparse decompositions expose systematic differences in encoded information, ranging from urban structures to broader biome and climate signals, and pretraining-space saliency maps further highlight complementary features such as roads and landmarks.

seltz.title: How to Use AlphaEarth for Similarity Search in Google Earth Engine
seltz.snippet:
Embeddings have transformed how we search text, images, and code. Instead of matching keywords, you compare vectors, which are numerical representations that capture meaning. Similar items end up close together, making it easy to find matches.

The same idea now works for geography, thanks to Google DeepMind’s AlphaEarth foundation model.

With a few reference coordinates and a few lines of code, you can search the entire planet for environmentally similar locations. Think of it like semantic search, but for places instead of text. Rather than asking "what documents are similar to this query?", you're asking "what locations are similar to these coordinates?"

In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to run a few-shot similarity search on satellite data at planetary scale. You'll extract embeddings, compute similarity scores, and validate your results with cross-validation. These are core ML techniques you can apply to any "find more places like X" problem.

This technique is useful for:

- Finding suitable regions for crops, reforestation, or renewable energy

- Identifying expansion sites that match successful existing locations

- Conservation planning based on environmental analogs

You'll use AlphaEarth embeddings, which encode the entire planet as 64-dimensional vectors summarizing a full year of satellite observations. If you have some reference points, you can make a global query.

I'll walk you through the process using Hass avocado farms as an example, but you can apply the same approach to any similarity search problem.

AlphaEarth is not a satellite. It's a foundation model trained on Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2, Landsat, GEDI LiDAR, MODIS, ERA5 climate reanalysis and dozens of other public Earth observation streams. The model compresses all of that into a single continuous-time embedding per 10m pixel, per year. ultimate.title: Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
ultimate.snippet: Ecological monitoring, carbon accounting and biodiversity assessment increasingly rely on annual Earth embeddings--learned vectors that compress a year of satellite observation for every ten-meter pixel on Earth, consumed in place of the imagery itself. What these vectors mean has not been established. Here we decompose two widely used embedding products and show that they contain individual ecological features, including fire, forest clearing and crop type, validated against independent reference data on events across six continents. The recovered concepts date abrupt canopy loss to the first post-disturbance growing season and resolve severity well enough to separate prescribed fire from wildfire. Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.

ultimate.title: Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
ultimate.snippet:
Here we decompose the two publicly available global embedding products, Tessera [8] and AlphaEarth [9], with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) [27, 28], a method developed to interpret language models. An SAE rewrites each embedding as a weighted combination of a few features, chosen from a learned set with many more features than the embedding has dimensions. Because each pixel can use only a few features, each feature tends to specialize on one surface condition, unlike principal components, which mix many. We test whether a feature records a phenomenon by when it appears, since a feature that represents fire should activate on burned pixels in the year of a mapped fire or after, and not before.

We decomposed two annual embedding products into named features and verified them against external reference data. By doing so, we found that annual Earth embeddings are interpretable records of the land surface. They record abrupt canopy change, resolve its severity, and date it to the calendar year containing the first growing season after the disturbance. The findings follow ecological intuition, which is consistent with the decomposition capturing real structure rather than artifacts of the method. Had it produced incoherent features like burn features peaking before fires, or a clean separation of causes that leave identical surface signals, either would have pointed to artifacts of the method. Representations that are already widely used can thus be decomposed into physically interpretable features and checked against independent data.

ultimate.snippet:
An annual Earth embedding is a learned per-pixel vector summarizing a year of satellite data. Its signal for any given event is spread across many dimensions, so no single dimension plainly means "fire." The authors decompose the vectors with a sparse autoencoder, a method that represents each vector using a small number of active directions chosen from a larger learned dictionary. Each direction is a *feature*, and its nonnegative weight at a pixel is its *activation*. For Tessera in the Dixie example, the dictionary has 1,024 features with 16 active per pixel.
Training uses embeddings alone, with no labels, reference maps or event dates, so the decomposition is never taught to look for fire.

#### AlphaEarth Foundations
[2] is the model that produced the Google Satellite Embedding dataset, whose D=64 embeddings we use. It treats the imagery of a location as a video: an encoder with spatial and temporal self-attention summarises all observations of a year into one unit-norm embedding per 10 m pixel. During training, decoders reconstruct from this summary the trajectories of many sources over the same period: optical multispectral imagery (Sentinel-2 and Landsat), synthetic-aperture radar (Sentinel-1), GEDI spaceborne lidar, MODIS land-surface temperature, ERA5 climate reanalysis, digital elevation and label maps; the embedding is also aligned with text. To produce the released embeddings, however, the trained encoder is applied to Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery only.

# Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
Robin Young, Srinivasan Keshav
## Abstract
Ecological monitoring, carbon accounting and biodiversity assessment increasingly rely on annual Earth embeddings--learned vectors that compress a year of satellite observation for every ten-meter pixel on Earth, consumed in place of the imagery itself. What these vectors mean has not been established. Here we decompose two widely used embedding products and show that they contain individual ecological features, including fire, forest clearing and crop type, validated against independent reference data on events across six continents. The recovered concepts date abrupt canopy loss to the first post-disturbance growing season and resolve severity well enough to separate prescribed fire from wildfire. Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.

ultimate.title: Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface | Cool Papers
ultimate.snippet: Ecological monitoring, carbon accounting and biodiversity assessment increasingly rely on annual Earth embeddings--learned vectors that compress a year of satellite observation for every ten-meter pixel on Earth, consumed in place of the imagery itself. What these vectors mean has not been established. Here we decompose two widely used embedding products and show that they contain individual ecological features, including fire, forest clearing and crop type, validated against independent reference data on events across six continents. The recovered concepts date abrupt canopy loss to the first post-disturbance growing season and resolve severity well enough to separate prescribed fire from wildfire. Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.

you.snippet:
We decomposed two annual embedding products into named features and verified them against external reference data. By doing so, we found that annual Earth embeddings are interpretable records of the land surface. They record abrupt canopy change, resolve its severity, and date it to the calendar year containing the first growing season after the disturbance.
Do Earth embeddings contain features that correspond to identifiable surface phenomena and can be verified against independent maps? If so, what do those features record about a disturbance, such as when it occurred, how severe it was or what caused it? And do different embedding products, trained on largely the same observations of Earth, contain the same phenomena? Here we decompose the two publicly available global embedding products, Tessera [8] and AlphaEarth [9], with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) [27, 28], a method developed to interpret language models.
Supplementary Information Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface
The embeddings record what a disturbance did to the surface, not what caused it, so they separate causes only when the surfaces differ. Fire does leave a distinct surface, and accordingly the western US burn family responds to European fires but not to European harvest or windthrow (Supplementary Note S9). Two further experiments demonstrate the temporal limits of decomposing annual embeddings.

you.title: Earth Embeddings · Pith Review
you.snippet:
The paper's central claim is that the reusable vector output of Earth-observation models—an Earth embedding—has become a product category in its own right, decoupled from the imagery and models that produced it. It argues the field should be understood as a landscape of three families: implicit location encoders that map coordinates directly to vectors without requiring imagery at inference time; patch embeddings that summarize mosaics or tiles; and pixel embeddings that produce dense per-pixel vectors from time series.
Surveying the available products and the studies that use them, the chapter concludes that explicit pixel embeddings currently have the strongest experimental support for land-cover-like mapping and spatial prediction, that semantic search is promising but under-benchmarked, and that time-series tasks remain weakly evaluated.
If the task-dependence conclusion holds, the community's next step should be a standardized embedding index with metadata and uncertainty layers, not a quest for one universal model. The terrestrial and Sentinel/Landsat bias of existing products makes ocean, atmospheric, snow, and infrastructure embeddings a natural, testable next frontier.
Who this is for: practitioners choosing an embedding product, grad students needing a map of the field, and referees who want to check whether a paper's claims about embeddings generally align with the current product landscape.
